Argument-specific rules held: kalam begins-to-exist, fine-tuning data-conceded/design-inferred (never 'scientists agree it's designed'), laws describe-not-prescribe, miracles possible-not-proven. Single-gate (Science&Faith).

Rules held: kalam begins-to-exist; morality duties-need-a-ground + 'atheists can be good'; evil = Plantinga consistency-not-proof + no tidy theodicy + redemptive anchor; contingency/Five Ways/ontological = philosophical terminus not the Nicene God.

Rules held: manuscripts=preservation-not-truth, archaeology=setting-not-message, canon recognized-not-invented + Apocrypha un-adjudicated, prophecy cumulative-not-mathematical, typology retrospective.

DUAL-CONSENSUS: apologia-argument all SOUND + apologia-orthodoxy CLEAN-after-fix (uniqueness 'exalted soul'->'soul merely taken up to heaven') + apologia-neutrality CLEAN (2 POLISH applied: hist_jesus mythicism credential-concede; appearances force-the-conclusion clarity). Rules held: 1 Cor 15 creed lead; disciples-had-experiences bounded (never 'resurrection proven'); martyrdom=sincerity-not-truth; bodily resurrection affirmed; copycat fails as mainstream judgment.

bigbang.Stating the Argument Carefully: Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began, so it has a cause—not yet God.
bigbang.The Science Behind “The Universe Began”: Expansion, the CMB, and light-element ratios converge on a cosmic beginning—though not a proven first instant.
bigbang.From a Beginning to a Cause: A beginning points to a transcendent, immaterial, powerful cause—its personhood a further, contested inference.
bigbang.The Live Alternatives, Taken Seriously: Serious alternatives to a beginning exist, but each smuggles in a structured “something” or faces real pressure.
bigbang.Where the Debate Actually Stands: The hot Big Bang is undisputed; whether the past boundary is a true beginning remains contested.
bigbang.What This Does and Does Not Establish: It doesn't prove God, but overturns the old default of an eternal, self-existing universe—a beginning that cries out for a cause.

cosmic.Stating the Question Carefully: The physical data are conceded; that purpose best explains them is a contested inference, not proof.
cosmic.How the Argument Developed: Design reasoning runs from Aristotle to a modern cosmic version built on order, intelligibility, and entropy.
cosmic.The First Strand: An Improbably Ordered: The universe's low-entropy beginning is astonishingly special—the kind of order a purposing mind might supply.
cosmic.The Second Strand: A Universe That Can B: That the cosmos is intelligible to minds fits a rational Creator better than blind chance.
cosmic.The Third Strand: A Cosmos Built to Be D: Habitability seems to correlate with discoverability—suggestive of purpose, though this is the most contested strand.
cosmic.The Strongest Objections: Anthropic selection, the multiverse, and cosmic waste each strike real blows—but carry their own unpaid costs.
cosmic.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The physics is undisputed; its interpretation is genuinely split, and no view is cost-free.
cosmic.What It Does, and Does Not, Establish: At most it points to a rational mind behind the cosmos—defensible, but honestly resistible.

laws.Stating the Question Carefully: The metaphysical question—why any order exists—points, as best explanation and not proof, toward a Mind.
laws.What Philosophers Mean by “a Law of Natu: Laws may be mere descriptions or genuine governors; the deep puzzle of order survives either view.
laws.The Argument’s Long History: The very idea of universal law arose within a theistic frame and was later sharpened philosophically.
laws.Premise 1: The Cosmos Is Deeply, Intelli: Nature is uniformly, mathematically ordered and—strangely—intelligible to minds; this premise is barely disputed.
laws.The Contingency of the Particular Laws: The particular laws appear contingent—could have been otherwise—which invites, contestably, a demand for explanation.
laws.Premise 2: Why a Mind Explains This Bett: The theist argues a rational Mind is a better terminus for cosmic order than an unexplained brute fact—a comparative claim, not a proof.
laws.The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full: Laws describe, not prescribe, so “who made them?” may be a category mistake; every worldview stops somewhere.
laws.The Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Car: Even granting laws are mere descriptions, why the cosmos is orderly at all still needs explaining.
laws.The Multiverse and the “Final Theory” Re: A multiverse only relocates the order, and a final theory still wouldn't breathe fire into equations.
laws.The Honest State of Scholarship: The metaphysics of laws is unsettled; the theistic reading is a respectable minority, not consensus.
laws.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: It doesn't prove God, but cosmic order is more at home with a Mind than without.

mathematics.Wigner Names the Puzzle: Wigner called mathematics' effectiveness in physics a mysterious gift with “no rational explanation.”
mathematics.The Argument, Stated Carefully: Math's uncanny fit with the world is some evidence—not proof—of a rational mind behind reality.
mathematics.The Evidence: When Pure Mathematics Arri: Pure mathematics repeatedly predicted unseen physical reality—the predictive cases are hardest to explain away.
mathematics.Four Philosophies of Mathematics—and Why: No philosophy of mathematics—Platonist, nominalist, fictionalist, or structuralist—dissolves the puzzle of its effectiveness.
mathematics.The Theistic Proposal: If reality flows from a rational Creator, its intelligibility and our grasp of it are expected, not lucky.
mathematics.The Strongest Objections—Stated at Full: The strongest objections cap or relocate the puzzle of mathematical effectiveness, but none pays it off.
mathematics.The Indispensability Debate, and an Hone: How real mathematics is remains disputed—and the argument is stronger the more real it is.
mathematics.The State of the Scholarship: The effectiveness is undisputed; its explanation is wide open, and the theistic reading is one serious option.
mathematics.What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Es: It doesn't prove God, but a world written in reason is more at home with a Mind.

originlife.What Abiogenesis Must Explain: Abiogenesis must explain metabolism, replication, and—deepest of all—the origin of specified biological information.
originlife.The Experimental Program, and Its Limits: Real experimental progress notwithstanding, no program has bridged chemistry to a coded, self-replicating cell.
originlife.The Design Inference from Information: Intelligence is the only known source of specified information, making design the best current explanation—defeasibly.
originlife.Steelmanning the Mainstream Program: The god-of-the-gaps charge, disputed probability numbers, and unknown early conditions are serious objections honestly conceded.
originlife.The State of the Scholarship: There's no consensus origin-of-life mechanism, but none is proven impossible; design remains a minority view.
originlife.What the Argument Does and Doesn’t Estab: It doesn't prove design, but shows life's information is a real mystery whose only known source is mind.

cambrian.What the “Explosion” Actually Is: Most major animal body plans appear in a geologically short Cambrian window—a real, agreed-upon event.
cambrian.Darwin’s Doubt—and Whose Doubt It Was: Darwin himself conceded the puzzle; Meyer reframes it as the origin of new biological information.
cambrian.The Case for the Premises, at Its Strong: The explosion is real and partly unexplained; the case leans on rare protein folds and rigid developmental networks.
cambrian.The Mainstream Reply, Stated Fairly and: Most biologists answer with a longer timeline, deeper divergences, patchy preservation, and rewiring of existing genes.
cambrian.Weighing the Exchange Honestly: Design fastens onto a real open problem, but its empirical premises are softer and more contested than its rhetoric.
cambrian.The Honest State of the Question: The data are agreed; the design inference is contested, not consensus, and rests on disputed estimates.
cambrian.Conclusion: What It Does and Does Not Sh: It doesn't refute evolution or prove design, but raises a serious challenge best held with humility.

privileged.Stating the Thesis Carefully: The conditions for life may also make the cosmos knowable—a checkable claim, with design a separate, contested inference.
privileged.How the Idea Developed: Building on the secular “Rare Earth” work, Gonzalez and Richards added that habitability also aids discovery.
privileged.Premise 1: Does the Correlation Hold?: The habitability–discoverability correlation is suggestive but under-tested—a pattern, not a demonstrated theorem.
privileged.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: Critics answer with observer selection, cherry-picking, unfalsifiability, and the Copernican principle of mediocrity.
privileged.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: Selection can't explain the cosmos's surplus intelligibility, but the correlation stays under-quantified—a clue, not a proof.
privileged.The Honest State of the Debate: Habitability science is respectable; the measurability correlation isn't mainstream, and most astronomers reject it.
privileged.Conclusion: What the Thesis Does and Doe: It doesn't prove design, but the cosmos being knowable, not just livable, fits theism as a modest clue.

finetuning.The Numbers That Stopped the Physicists: The physical constants sit in eerily narrow life-permitting ranges—arithmetic that unsettled even hardened physicists.
finetuning.What Fine-Tuning Actually Means: Fine-tuning means the fundamental constants lie in ranges so slim small changes would forbid life's chemistry.
finetuning.Three Doors: Chance, Necessity, Design: Chance, necessity, or design; by the likelihood principle fine-tuning tilts toward design—confirmation, not proof.
finetuning.The Strongest Objections: The multiverse, the anthropic “puddle,” and the measure problem are the argument's strongest challenges.
finetuning.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The data are undisputed; the interpretation is contested, and design earns a seat among serious explanations.
finetuning.What It Does, and Does Not, Establish: It points at most to a fine-tuner, never “scientists agree it's designed”—defensible, but honestly resistible.

miracles.Stating the Question Carefully: Keep possibility (philosophy) apart from actuality (evidence); the a priori bar on miracles is what's contested.
miracles.What a Miracle Is—and Is Not: A miracle is a special act of God transcending nature—a coherent concept, even to atheists like Flew.
miracles.Descriptions, Not Prescriptions: Laws describe how things behave when nothing interferes; an agent introducing a new cause violates nothing.
miracles.The Closed Box and the Open One: Whether the universe is causally closed is a metaphysical assumption, not a scientific finding.
miracles.Spinoza: Miracles as an Absurdity: Spinoza's impossibility argument begs the question and works only given his pantheism, which no theist holds.
miracles.Hume: Miracles as Never Credible: Hume argued no testimony could ever make a miracle credible—a serious objection to weigh honestly, not to mock.
miracles.Where Hume’s Argument Breaks Down: Hume fails three ways: rare events can be well-attested, “uniform experience” is circular, and his weighing is skewed.
miracles.The State of the Scholarship: The confident a priori dismissal has collapsed; the debate has moved to weighing evidence case by case.
miracles.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: This only unbars the door: miracles are possible and worth investigating, never that any actually occurred.

thomistic.The Hand, the Stick, and the Stone: Aquinas's whole case hangs on the kind of causal series he means — misread it and you refute a phantom.
thomistic.The Five Ways in Brief: The Five Ways sketch five routes to God as the world's ultimate source; the First Way is the paradigm.
thomistic.The Single Most Important Point: The series is simultaneous and here-and-now, requiring a present sustainer, not a first event long ago.
thomistic.The Metaphysics Beneath the First Way: Change is a potential becoming actual, and only something purely actual can ground the chain.
thomistic.The Objections — Steelmanned: Aquinas never claimed everything has a cause; the inertia objection is the one demanding a real reply.
thomistic.The Honest State of the Scholarship: There is no consensus either way, but the lazy dismissals of the argument no longer survive.
thomistic.What the Five Ways Do and Do Not Establi: If sound, the Ways reach a sustaining first cause — not yet the good, personal, triune God.

kalam.A question that refuses to stay small: Either the universe is eternal or it began — and which it is changes everything.
kalam.The argument, stated with care: Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began; so it has a cause.
kalam.Premise 1: out of nothing, nothing comes: Being does not arise from non-being; the quantum vacuum is something, not nothing.
kalam.Premise 2: the case for a beginning: Both philosophy and cosmology point to a beginning, though the science corroborates rather than proves it.
kalam.From a cause to a Creator: The cause must be spaceless, timeless, immaterial, powerful, and plausibly a personal mind.
kalam.The strongest objections, fairly stated: 'What caused God?' misreads premise 1, but critics like Morriston and Oppy keep the debate open.
kalam.The honest state of the debate: The argument stays live and contested; the step from cause to person is most disputed.
kalam.What Kalam does and does not establish: Kalam makes a serious case for a transcendent cause, not a proof of any particular God.

leibniz.The Most Persistent Question: The question 'why is there anything at all?' stands whether or not the universe began.
leibniz.The Argument, Stated Carefully: A contingent universe needs an explanation beyond itself: a necessary, transcendent being.
leibniz.The Strongest Objections: The deepest objections attack the Principle of Sufficient Reason and offer the cosmos as a brute stopping point.
leibniz.The Honest State of the Scholarship: Philosophers still divide over the PSR and whether the universe can simply be 'just there.'
leibniz.What It Does, and Doesn't, Establish: If sound, it reaches a necessary ground of being — one strand toward, not yet, the personal God.

beauty.The Datum: Beauty in Nature, Art, and Nu: Beauty in nature, art, and mathematics is a real datum any worldview must explain.
beauty.The Argument and Its History: Beauty fits more naturally with a Creator who is its source than with blind matter.
beauty.The Case at Its Strongest: The convergence of beauty, elegant laws, and minds that delight in them favors one Author.
beauty.The Objections, Steelmanned: Evolution, aesthetic subjectivism, and nature's ugliness each press hard against the argument.
beauty.Replies — and Honest Concessions: Real replies exist, but beauty's objectivity is contested and nature's ugliness blunts the argument's edge.
beauty.The State of Scholarship: Even its defenders treat beauty as one modest strand, not a stand-alone proof.
beauty.Conclusion: What It Does and Does Not Es: Beauty does not prove God, but theism explains it more gracefully than naturalism does.

consciousness.The Hard Problem: Why physical processes are accompanied by inner experience resists ordinary scientific reduction.
consciousness.The Argument Stated: Consciousness is more expected if reality is grounded in Mind than in blind matter.
consciousness.The Force of the Argument: Naturalism explains the mental by the non-mental — but consciousness is what will not reduce.
consciousness.Objections, Stated at Full Strength: Even if materialism fails, panpsychism and naturalistic dualism, not only God, remain live options.
consciousness.The State of the Scholarship: The hard problem is taken seriously, yet physicalism persists and this is no proof of God.
consciousness.Conclusion: What It Establishes, and Wha: Consciousness favors a mental ground over pure physicalism — a clue, not a proof.

desire.The argument stated: A longing nothing earthly satisfies is best explained, Lewis says, by our being made for more.
desire.The longing and its history: The restless longing Lewis called Joy runs from Augustine and Aquinas through Romanticism.
desire.Why the argument has force: Natural desires reliably track real objects, so a universal longing aimed at nothing would be strange.
desire.The objections, stated at full strength: Wanting something does not make it exist, and critics call the natural/artificial distinction rigged.
desire.Replying—while conceding what must be co: It is no proof; the case rests on the peculiar shape of a longing survival cannot fully explain.
desire.The state of the question: Philosophers treat the argument as serious but minor — a contributor, not a decisive proof.
desire.What it does, and does not, establish: It does not prove God, but argues our longing is as well explained by design as by mistake.

reason.The Argument Stated: If our beliefs are merely the products of non-rational causes, the naturalist has no reason to trust his own reasoning.
reason.A History of an Idea: From Balfour and Haldane to Lewis, thinkers pressed that naturalism undercuts trust in reason.
reason.Plantinga's Rigorous Cousin: Plantinga argues naturalism plus evolution gives us a defeater for trusting our own minds.
reason.The Strongest Objections: Anscombe's level distinction and the 'true beliefs aid survival' reply are the strongest challenges.
reason.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The argument is unresolved — a live problem for naturalism, not a settled refutation.
reason.What It Does — and Does Not — Establish: It is a problem for naturalism, not a proof of God — reason fits a rational source better.

religious.The claim, stated carefully: An apparent experience of God carries genuine, defeasible weight — not proof, but evidence.
religious.Two modern defenses: Swinburne and Alsto: Swinburne and Alston argue religious experience deserves the same default trust we give perception.
religious.The objections, taken at full strength: Neuroscience, conflicting religious claims, and Freud's projection are the serious objections — diversity the strongest.
religious.The honest state of the question: Experience cannot settle which God is real, but gives the experiencer genuine, non-dismissable warrant.

ontological.The Argument That Tries to Reach God by: The ontological argument tries to reach God from the bare concept of God alone.
ontological.Anselm's Original: Greatness That Cannot: Anselm argues the greatest conceivable being cannot coherently be thought of as failing to exist.
ontological.Descartes: Existence as a Perfection: Descartes treats existence as a perfection the supremely perfect being must possess.
ontological.The Modern Modal Version: Plantinga: If a maximally great being is even possible, Plantinga argues, it exists necessarily.
ontological.The Strongest Objections: Kant retired the older forms; the modal version stalls on whether God is even possible.
ontological.What Plantinga Actually Claimed: Plantinga claimed only that the argument shows theistic belief is rational, not that it proves God.
ontological.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The argument is valid; the whole debate now rests on the contested possibility premise.
ontological.Conclusion: What It Does and Doesn't Est: It does not prove God, but shows a maximally great being is either necessary or impossible.

moral.The Argument and Its History: If objective moral duties are real, they need a ground beyond human opinion.
moral.Premise 2: That Some Things Are Really W: That some acts are really wrong is a properly basic conviction shared even by secular realists.
moral.Premise 1: What Grounds the Moral Law?: The claim is not that atheists cannot be good, but that objective morality needs grounding in God's nature.
moral.The Euthyphro Dilemma: Goodness is neither arbitrary command nor a standard above God, but God's own necessary nature.
moral.The Strongest Objection: Wielenberg's Go: Wielenberg grounds morality in brute necessary facts; the theist replies duties must be owed to someone.
moral.The Darwinian Dilemma — Which Cuts Both: Evolutionary debunking of moral intuitions cuts against secular realism at least as hard as theism.
moral.What the Argument Does, and Does Not, Es: If sound, it reaches a good lawgiver — not the full Christian God — never impugning atheists' goodness.

evil.Stating the problem at its strongest: The problem comes in three forms — logical, evidential, and existential — of rising difficulty.
evil.The logical problem, and why most philos: Plantinga's defense shows God and evil can consistently coexist — not why evil exists, only that it can.
evil.The evidential problem: the genuinely ha: The hard version asks whether pointless suffering makes God unlikely; no reply is tidy or complete.
evil.The cross: not a theodicy but a presence: Christianity offers not a tidy explanation but a God who entered suffering and promises to defeat it.
evil.The critic's last word — and a reply: The skeptic's intuition retains real weight; the theist's reply is a defensible reframing that keeps faith reasonable, not a claimed victory.
evil.The honest state of the question: The logical problem failed and the evidential remains unresolved — but the grief no argument can relieve is met by the God who entered it.

manuscript.Stating the Question Carefully: The question is whether we can recover what the authors wrote—not whether it's true.
manuscript.How the Argument Developed: Textual criticism turned the classical method onto the New Testament; early apologists overstated its reach.
manuscript.Premise 1: Why Abundance and Antiquity M: Many independent, branching copies expose each other's errors, letting scholars triangulate the original.
manuscript.Premise 2: Does the New Testament Actual: The New Testament's witnesses are unusually early and abundant, and show real copying stability.
manuscript.The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full: Ehrman: hundreds of thousands of variants, some deliberate theological changes, and an early fluid text.
manuscript.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: Variants abound because copies do; under 1% matter, and no doctrine hangs on them.
manuscript.The Honest State of Scholarship: Scholars broadly agree the text is well recovered; the live debates are narrow and technical.
manuscript.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: The manuscripts show the text was accurately preserved—not that its contents are true.

earlydate.Stating the Argument Carefully: An early date starves legend; the strongest case rests on Paul's letters and creeds.
earlydate.Premise One: An Early Date Starves a Leg: While eyewitnesses and hostile witnesses live, invented claims can be checked and challenged.
earlydate.Premise Two: The New Testament Really Is: The 1 Corinthians 15 creed and Paul's letters place the core claims strikingly early.
earlydate.The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full: Most scholars date the Gospels 70–95, reading Jesus' Jerusalem prophecy as written after the event.
earlydate.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: The prophecy is vague and Acts' silences telling, but the early creed stands regardless.
earlydate.The Honest State of the Scholarship: Gospel dating stays contested, but scholars broadly agree the earliest tradition is remarkably early.
earlydate.Conclusion: What Early Dating Does and D: Early dating rules out slow legend—but early is not the same as true.

eyewitnesses.Stating the Claim Carefully: The claim is that the traditions trace to eyewitnesses—not that apostles signed the Gospels.
eyewitnesses.How the Question Was Framed—and Reframed: Form critics saw anonymous folklore; Bauckham reframed the Gospels as rooted in eyewitness testimony.
eyewitnesses.The Case, Built in Three Strands: Named minor characters, the right name frequencies, and early testimony point to eyewitness sources.
eyewitnesses.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: Critics: memory distorts over decades, and the onomastic and inclusio arguments remain contested.
eyewitnesses.The Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Car: Memory holds for central events, and embarrassing details survive—though the inclusio should be held lightly.
eyewitnesses.The Honest State of Scholarship: The late-legend thesis is now the harder case, but eyewitness accuracy remains contested.
eyewitnesses.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: The Gospels read like testimony deserving a hearing—not proof of authorship or the miracles.

names.Stating the Argument Carefully: Name frequencies are local and time-bound; the Gospel names match first-century Palestine.
names.How the Argument Developed: Ilan catalogued Palestinian Jewish names; Bauckham tested the Gospels against that independent baseline.
names.Premise 1: Why Name Frequency Is a Water: Name frequencies leak unconsciously from real life and are nearly impossible to fake.
names.Premise 2: Do the Gospel Names Actually: The Gospel names, ratios, and disambiguation habits match Palestine, not the diaspora.
names.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: Critics: the sample is small, and a well-informed outsider could reproduce the names.
names.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: The fit is real and unfaked, though it points to provenance, not proven eyewitnesses.
names.The Honest State of Scholarship: The Palestinian match is accepted; how much it proves remains an ongoing debate.
names.Conclusion: What the Names Do and Do Not: The names establish early Palestinian provenance—not authorship, the events, or the miracles.

jewishness.Stating the Argument Carefully: Jesus' thoroughly Jewish portrait points to early Palestinian origin—a claim about provenance, not truth.
jewishness.How the Argument Developed: From the His: The Hellenistic-myth thesis collapsed; scholars now recover Jesus firmly within first-century Judaism.
jewishness.Premise 1: The Texture of the Portrait: Incidental detail—legal debates, Aramaic phrases, names—fits pre-70 Palestine, not a later world.
jewishness.Premise 2: Why Invention Is the Worse Ex: Invention is unlikely: the awkward Jewishness and vanished pre-war world resist later reconstruction.
jewishness.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: A skilled Jewish author could write a convincing Jesus—and authentic setting proves no miracle.
jewishness.The Replies—and What They Can and Cannot: Frictions and pre-70 detail resist invention, yet authentic setting still cannot prove the events.
jewishness.The Honest State of Scholarship: Early Palestinian provenance is near-settled; the leap to reliable events stays contested.
jewishness.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: The Jewish Jesus is early and authentic—but that proves provenance, not the miracles.

coincidences.Stating the Argument Carefully: Casual, unplanned interlocks between accounts suggest independent reports—a cumulative inference, not a proof.
coincidences.How the Argument Developed: Paley and Blunt pioneered the argument; the McGrews revived it with probabilistic rigor.
coincidences.Premise 1: Why Unintended Interlocking P: Uncoordinated, incidental agreement is far likelier from real knowledge than from fabrication.
coincidences.Premise 2: Are There Really Many Such Ca: Cases range from strong—Philip, Herod's court, Acts and the Epistles—to weaker ones.
coincidences.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: Carrier: shared sources and literary dependence explain the fits; defenders ignore the misses.
coincidences.A Reply — and What It Can and Cannot Car: Redaction predicts the wrong shape; the strongest cases survive, though weak ones must be dropped.
coincidences.The Honest State of the Scholarship: The revived argument is little-engaged academically—promising and suggestive, but genuinely contested.
coincidences.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: The interlocks point to well-informed, independent sources—not to inerrancy or the miracles.

consistency.Stating the Question Carefully: The Bible is a library, and a difference is not a contradiction—nor would consistency prove truth.
consistency.How the Argument Developed: From Augustine's harmony to today's Ehrman-versus-Licona poles, the difficulty is old and seriously answered.
consistency.The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full: Ehrman: read the accounts side by side and real discrepancies appear that harmonizing only papers over.
consistency.A Reply—by Genre, Perspective, and Ancie: Ancient biography's conventions explain most differences as complementary—while the hardest cases are honestly conceded.
consistency.The Critic’s Last Word—and the Reply: Accuracy is genre-relative; surface variation over a shared core is what honest testimony looks like.
consistency.The Honest State of Scholarship: Scholars remain genuinely divided, but neither 'seamless' nor 'hopeless tangle' has real support.
consistency.Conclusion: What Consistency Does and Do: Consistency removes the contradiction charge but does not, by itself, prove the contents true.

canon.Stating the Question Carefully: How the canon formed—recognized, not invented—is a separate question from whether it is inspired.
canon.How the Canon Actually Formed: A Timelin: The canon emerged gradually over centuries; its core was received early, long before any council.
canon.Premise 1: The Criteria Were Principled,: The church tested books by apostolicity, orthodoxy, and widespread use—as if discovering, not deciding.
canon.Premise 2: A Functioning Core Long Befor: The four Gospels and Paul functioned as Scripture early; only the margins were ever disputed.
canon.Treating the Disputed Books Honestly: Some books were genuinely doubted for generations—evidence of careful sifting, not rubber-stamping.
canon.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: Ehrman: early Christianity was diverse, orthodoxy simply won, and the criteria look circular.
canon.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: The rejected gospels are demonstrably later; diversity is compatible with a genuinely principled sorting.
canon.Denominational Differences: A Fair State: Catholics, Orthodox, and Protestants differ over the Old Testament deuterocanonical books (the “Apocrypha”)—a disagreement this essay won't adjudicate.
canon.The Honest State of Scholarship: Historians agree no council created the canon; only refined questions of timing remain.
canon.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: The canon was recognized, not invented—but recognition does not by itself prove it inspired.

archaeology.Stating the Question Carefully: Archaeology cannot excavate a miracle; it tests the Bible's checkable setting, not its message.
archaeology.How the Argument Developed: Albright and Sherwin-White vindicated the biblical framework—of setting and persons, not theology.
archaeology.Premise 1: Why Incidental Accuracy Earns: Getting shifting titles and local details right signals a well-informed author close to events.
archaeology.Premise 2: The Confirmations, at Their S: Named persons and physical sites—House of David, Pilate, Belshazzar—repeatedly confirm the Bible's setting.
archaeology.The Strongest Objections, Stated at Full: Critics: the spade contradicts the text on the Exodus, conquest, and united monarchy's scale.
archaeology.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: Minimalism overreaches, and the confirmations are real—but archaeology yields no grand monarchy or conquest.
archaeology.The Honest State of Scholarship: Scholarship is a spectrum; neither 'proves the Bible' nor 'worthless' has serious support.
archaeology.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: The writers knew their world; a reliable setting is not proof of every event or the theology.

deadseascrolls.Stating the Question Carefully: The Scrolls test transmission, not truth; they are pre-Christian, Jewish, and contain no New Testament.
deadseascrolls.How the Argument Developed: The Isaiah comparison launched the case; later scholarship gave a fuller, more honest picture.
deadseascrolls.Premise 1: A Thousand-Year Leap Backward: The Scrolls push our copies a thousand years earlier, before Christ, across nearly every book.
deadseascrolls.Premise 2: How Stable Was the Text—Reall: A recognizable text stayed stable, though several text-streams coexisted before the text was standardized.
deadseascrolls.The Strongest Objection, Stated at Full: Tov: the text was pluriform—Jeremiah existed in two editions—so 'never changed' is false.
deadseascrolls.A Reply—and What It Can and Cannot Carry: The variation is bounded, and the stream that became our Bible was copied faithfully.
deadseascrolls.The Honest State of Scholarship: Scholars agree on both real pluriformity and faithful transmission of the stream that endured.
deadseascrolls.Conclusion: What This Does and Does Not: The Old Testament was faithfully preserved—not proven true, and not literally 'never changed.'

prophecy.Stating the Argument Carefully: Fulfilled prophecy is a cumulative inference, defended at two hinges: dating and the inference itself.
prophecy.How the Argument Developed: Prophecy is the oldest Christian argument; Stoner's statistical one-in-10^17 version should be retired.
prophecy.Premise 2 First: Did the Predictions Rea: Isaiah, Micah, and the Psalms are provably pre-Christian—though Daniel's dating is genuinely disputed.
prophecy.The Genuinely Striking Cases: The strongest cases converge on uncontrivable details—birthplace, a rich man's burial, divided garments.
prophecy.The Honest Difficulty: Psalm 22:16: Psalm 22:16's 'pierced' reading is genuinely contested; the case should not rest on that word.
prophecy.The Inference Hinge: Three Objections at: Three objections: the texts are vague, self-fulfilled, or the story built from Scripture.
prophecy.The Hardest Cases: When the New Testamen: Some citations, like Hosea 11:1 and Isaiah 7:14, are typology, not strict prediction.
prophecy.The Suffering Servant: A Test Case: Isaiah 53's referent is genuinely contested; the individual-messiah reading is an ancient Jewish option.
prophecy.The Honest State of the Question: The texts are pre-Christian, but the inference divides scholars, and much usage is typological.
prophecy.Conclusion: What Fulfilled Prophecy Does: Fulfilled prophecy corroborates within a cumulative case; taken alone it does not compel.

daniel70.The Most Dangerous Verse to Calculate: Daniel's countdown is thrilling and contested; the task is neither to overclaim nor dismiss it.
daniel70.The Prophecy, Stated Carefully: Seventy 'sevens' likely means 490 years, and four buried questions decide its meaning.
daniel70.Four Questions That Decide Everything: The reading hinges on the decree, the anointed one, the year's length, and the final week.
daniel70.The Apologetic Argument: A Date with the: Conservative choices land on Jesus, and the prophecy's shape fits even without day-precise math.
daniel70.The Critical Reading, Steelmanned: Critics date Daniel to about 165 BC and read it of Onias III and Antiochus IV.
daniel70.Where the Apologist Must Concede: The 360-day year and the decree are contested; neither reading simply falls out of the text.
daniel70.The Reply: The dating isn't settled, and Jewish tradition itself tied Daniel's clock to the Second Temple's end.
daniel70.What It Establishes — and What It Doesn': Not a mathematical proof, but a suggestive fit: an anointed one cut off before AD 70.

messianic-prophecy.An Argument as Old as the Church Itself: Appealing to the prophets is the oldest Christian argument—and it must be made honestly.
messianic-prophecy.How to Read Prophecy Honestly: 'Fulfill' has several senses; the case rests on uncontrivable predictions, not typological or stageable ones.
messianic-prophecy.A Catalogue of the Prophecies: Lineage, birthplace, passion, and vindication converge on Jesus—with each text's strength honestly flagged.
messianic-prophecy.The Honest Objections: Retrojection is met by uncontrivable, pre-dated cases; the out-of-context texts are read as typology, and Stoner's odds are frankly retired.
messianic-prophecy.What the Argument Does — and Does Not —: The prophecies give a striking cumulative convergence, not a single knockdown mathematical proof.

typology.A Boy Carrying the Wood Up the Mountain: Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain is not a prediction—but it rhymes with Christ.
typology.What Typology Is — and What It Is Not: Typology reads real history as a pattern fulfilled in Christ—recognized retrospectively, practiced by the apostles.
typology.Persons Who Prefigure the Person: Adam, Isaac, Melchizedek and others foreshadow Christ—some named by the New Testament, some only thematic.
typology.Events and Institutions That Point Beyon: Passover, the wilderness gifts, and the temple all lean forward and find completion in Christ.
typology.The Three Offices That Converge: Israel kept prophet, priest, and king apart; in Jesus the three anointed offices converge.
typology.The Strongest Objection — Stated Fairly: Typology can seem to prove anything, and to read Christian conclusions back into Israel's Scriptures.
typology.The State of the Question: Typology has been rehabilitated; scholars debate its extent, not whether the New Testament uses it.
typology.What This Does — and Does Not — Establis: Typology proves nothing alone; it supplies coherence once you already trust the resurrection.

earlycreed.A Tradition Older Than the New Testament: In 1 Corinthians 15:3-7 Paul recites a fixed creed he received, older than his own letter.
earlycreed.The Marks of a Borrowed Formula: Handing-on language, non-Pauline wording, and creedal structure mark it as a pre-Pauline formula.
earlycreed.The Dating: Counting Backward From the C: Counting back through Paul's biography dates the creed to within a few years of the cross.
earlycreed.What the Creed Establishes: The death-burial-raised-appeared confession is bedrock from the start, too early for legend to grow.
earlycreed.What the Creed Does Not Establish: It proves early, sincere belief in the appearances, not by itself the resurrection.
earlycreed.The Strongest Objections: Skeptics grant the early belief but posit visions; those accounts leave key data unexplained.
earlycreed.The State of the Scholarship: The creed's early date is near-consensus, affirmed by believers and atheists alike.
earlycreed.Conclusion: The creed establishes an early, sincere witness and forecloses legend, the case's starting point.

minimalfacts.An Argument Designed to Survive Disagree: The case builds only on facts even skeptics grant, sidestepping debates over Scripture.
minimalfacts.The Two Criteria: A minimal fact must be strongly evidenced and granted by most scholars, skeptics included.
minimalfacts.From Facts to Resurrection: The Inferenc: Resurrection is inferred as the best explanation of the facts together, not a proof.
minimalfacts.The Strongest Objections: The strongest critiques target the method: worldview priors and the disputed consensus count.
minimalfacts.The State of the Scholarship: Scholars broadly grant the crucifixion and the disciples' sincere experiences; their cause stays contested.
minimalfacts.What the Argument Does and Doesn't Estab: It makes resurrection the best explanation for the open inquirer, not a coercive proof.

emptytomb.A claim that could be checked: The empty tomb was a public claim anyone in Jerusalem could have checked by looking.
emptytomb.The fact and its supports: Five converging lines of evidence support the empty tomb, cumulatively strong though none decisive alone.
emptytomb.What the evidence does and does not show: An empty tomb is a serious datum but does not, by itself, prove the resurrection.
emptytomb.The sceptical case, in its strongest for: The strongest objection denies any known tomb; Jewish law and archaeology tell against it.
emptytomb.Where the scholarship stands: The empty tomb is a strong, well-defended position, more probable than not but genuinely disputed.
emptytomb.Conclusion: The grave was, in all probability, found empty; what emptied it is the next question.

appearances.The claim that started a movement: Named witnesses insisted they saw Jesus alive after his execution, the movement's load-bearing claim.
appearances.The shape of the evidence: many sources,: The appearance reports span independent sources and widely varied circumstances, resisting one easy cause.
appearances.What the witnesses say they saw: Witnesses describe a bodily yet transformed Jesus, foreign to Jewish expectation and to tidy theories.
appearances.The hallucination hypothesis, in its str: The strongest naturalistic rival grants sincere belief and attributes the sightings to visions.
appearances.Why the hallucination theory cannot bear: Group settings, unprimed and hostile witnesses, and the empty tomb strain the vision theory badly.
appearances.The strongest counter-replies, taken ser: The critics' best replies still fail to match the full combination of the appearance data.
appearances.What the appearances do and do not estab: It establishes that many were convinced they saw Jesus alive, but does not by itself force the resurrection conclusion.

burial.The fact that has to come first: Before there can be an empty tomb, Jesus must first have a known, identifiable grave.
burial.The argument, stated carefully: Three premises conclude Jesus was buried in a known tomb, a location, not a miracle.
burial.Premise 1: the burial is early and multi: The burial stands in the early creed and independently across all four Gospels.
burial.Premise 2: nobody invents a Sanhedrist h: A burying Sanhedrist like Joseph of Arimathea is too awkward to have been invented.
burial.Premise 3: a burial was expected, not ex: Jewish law, Roman pragmatism, and a nailed heel bone show Jerusalem burials did happen.
burial.Why the burial is the foundation: The burial certifies the death and fixes a known location the resurrection claim could be checked against.
burial.The state of the question: The bare burial is broadly agreed; whether the tomb was known and locatable is debated.
burial.What the argument does and does not esta: It establishes a real death and identifiable tomb, not the empty tomb or resurrection.

disciplesbelief.A Question Almost Everyone Concedes: Believing and skeptical historians agree the disciples sincerely believed they had seen Jesus alive.
disciplesbelief.The Argument Stated: Five steps argue the resurrection best explains a belief no one was poised to invent.
disciplesbelief.A Belief No One in That World Was Poised: Jewish hope had no template for one man raised bodily in the middle of history.
disciplesbelief.Sincerity Sealed in Blood: The disciples' willingness to die proves their sincerity, ruling out fraud, not the belief's truth.
disciplesbelief.The Strongest Objections, Answered: Visions, cognitive dissonance, and naturalist priors each leave a conspicuous part unexplained.
disciplesbelief.The State of the Scholarship: The sincere early belief is widely granted; its cause is where the real debate lies.
disciplesbelief.What the Argument Does and Does Not Show: It doesn't prove the resurrection but shows the belief's origin resists naturalistic explanation.

respred.A Prophecy That Invites Its Own Refutati: Jesus' self-predicted death and vindication is a supporting strand, not a standalone proof.
respred.The Claim, Stated Carefully: Three strands suggest Jesus anticipated death and vindication, not clear proof-texts of Easter.
respred.The Case For Authenticity: Embarrassing framing and awkward, cryptic sayings point to an authentic pre-Easter core.
respred.The Strongest Objection: Prophecy After: The majority view holds the detailed predictions were sharpened after the fact by believers.
respred.The Reply — Without Overclaiming: Invention explains polished predictions poorly; a prophet expecting vindication survives the critical filter.
respred.The State of the Scholarship: There is no consensus that Jesus predicted his resurrection in specific, detailed terms.
respred.What This Does and Does Not Establish: A reasonable case that Jesus expected death and vindication, but not detailed foreknowledge.

postres.An Argument That Runs Backward: Start from the movement's undisputed behaviour and ask what cause best explains it.
postres.The First Datum: Men Who Would Not Take: Frightened deserters became bold proclaimers; their willingness to suffer shows sincerity, not truth.
postres.The Second Datum: Mutations in a Conserv: Monotheists suddenly worshipped a crucified man and reshaped their rites, mutations demanding a cause.
postres.The Third Datum: Growth in the Wrong Cit: The claim was proclaimed and grew fastest in Jerusalem, where a corpse could refute it.
postres.Putting the Inference Together: The pattern presses one question: what caused that belief so suddenly, early, and firmly?
postres.The Strongest Objections: Cognitive dissonance, gradual Christology, and borrowing each explain only fragments of the pattern.
postres.The State of the Scholarship: The behavioural facts are widely granted; the inference to a bodily resurrection is contested.
postres.What the Argument Does and Does Not Esta: It doesn't prove the resurrection alone but shows real effects the resurrection best explains.

uniqueness.An Inconvenient Easter: The resurrection claim violated Jewish expectation rather than confirming it, not a recycled myth.
uniqueness.The Claim, Stated Carefully: The claim is a bodily rising of Jesus, not a ghost, a metaphor, or a soul merely taken up to heaven.
uniqueness.Why the Bodily, Datable Character Matter: Its bodily, datable character anchors the claim in history, unlike a seasonal myth.
uniqueness.The Dying-and-Rising Gods: Under scholarly scrutiny the dying-and-rising-god parallel to Jesus collapses, even skeptics conclude so.
uniqueness.Heroes Taken Up: Romulus and Apollonius: Romulus and Apollonius are translated to heaven, not bodily raised, a different category entirely.
uniqueness.The Strongest Objections: Borrowing-from-fragments and the visionary theory are the best objections; both still fall short.
uniqueness.The State of the Question: Scholarship has abandoned Frazer; the claim's strangeness is granted, its origin still contested.
uniqueness.What Uniqueness Does and Does Not Prove: Uniqueness is not truth, but it dismantles the lazy 'just another old myth' dismissal.

sceptics.The brother who did not believe: James, a skeptical brother, became a martyr-leader of the church, what changed him?
sceptics.The logic of the hostile witness: A witness who testifies against his own prior convictions carries special evidential weight.
sceptics.What we actually know about James: Independent sources converge: James's unbelief, the creed's appearance to him, his leadership and death.
sceptics.The transformation that needs explaining: The grief-vision theory fits James poorly: he lacked the yearning such visions require.
sceptics.The naturalistic explanations, taken ser: Grief, dynastic ambition, and slow persuasion each fail to explain James's conversion.
sceptics.What the argument does — and does not —: It establishes a skeptic radically transformed; the resurrection is the inferred best explanation, not proof.
sceptics.The state of the question: James's basic facts are near-consensus; the live debate is why he converted.
sceptics.Conclusion: It doesn't prove the resurrection alone but hands the case a well-attested former doubter.

hist_jesus.The shape of the consensus: That Jesus existed is near-settled among historians, affirmed even by skeptics like Ehrman.
hist_jesus.The earliest witness: Paul: Paul, writing early, personally met Jesus' brother and Peter, a link hard to fabricate.
hist_jesus.The Gospels and the tradition behind the: The Gospels are late, but multiple independent tradition-streams converge behind them.
hist_jesus.The witnesses outside the church: Non-Christian sources like Tacitus and Josephus corroborate Jesus, though thinner than often claimed.
hist_jesus.The criteria that secure a core: Multiple attestation and embarrassing facts like the crucifixion anchor a real historical core.
hist_jesus.The strongest case for the other side: Mythicism — Carrier's credentialed, peer-reviewed best case — is serious-looking but has essentially no scholarly foothold.
hist_jesus.What this establishes, and what it does: The evidence establishes a real crucified man, not his divinity or resurrection.

multiatt.What the Criterion Claims: A fact found in independent sources is harder to explain as later invention.
multiatt.The Independent Source Streams: The method works only where sources are genuinely independent, not copying one another.
multiatt.The Turn Against the Criteria — Steelman: Many scholars now argue the criteria cannot cleanly separate authentic tradition from later interpretation.
multiatt.The Considered Reply: Demote, don't discard: attestation secures the broad portrait, not a saying's exact wording.
multiatt.The State of the Question: The field is in flux with no agreed replacement, so the better criteria still serve.
multiatt.Conclusion: What It Does and Doesn't Est: It doesn't prove Christianity but makes dismissing Jesus' broad historical outline very hard.
